subject: Chemistry

topics.title: Models of the particulate nature of matter
How much, how fast and how far?

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of introduction to the particulate nature of matter.
solution: Matter consists of particles whose arrangement, motion and attractions differ between solids, liquids and gases.
questions.subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in introduction to the particulate nature of matter.
solution: Heating raises average kinetic energy; a change of state occurs when energy changes intermolecular organization rather than chemical identity.
questions.subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to introduction to the particulate nature of matter.
solution: Gases are compressible because their particles occupy a small fraction of the container volume and are widely separated.
questions.subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of introduction to the particulate nature of matter to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Diffusion becomes faster at higher temperature because particles move faster on average.
questions.subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

questions.label: Hard
body: A sample contains 18.0 g H2O. Calculate the amount in moles using M = 18.0 g mol-1.
solution: n = m/M = 18.0 g / 18.0 g mol-1 = 1.00 mol.
questions.subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

questions.label: Medium
body: Identify and correct one common misconception about introduction to the particulate nature of matter.
solution:
For example, reject: Particles in a solid do not move at all.
Correct account: Matter consists of particles whose arrangement, motion and attractions differ between solids, liquids and gases.
questions.subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure the diffusion time of a coloured solute through water at different temperatures. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable.
solution:
Independent: water temperature.
Dependent: time for colour to reach a fixed distance.
Controlled: solute concentration and vessel geometry.
questions.subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

questions.label: Hard
body: Predict the trend expected in the investigation to measure the diffusion time of a coloured solute through water at different temperatures and explain its chemical basis.
solution:
Expected trend: diffusion time should decrease as temperature rises.
The explanation should use the model or relationship: Heating raises average kinetic energy; a change of state occurs when energy changes intermolecular organization rather than chemical identity.
questions.subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss introduction to the particulate nature of matter, integrating particulate or structural models, quantitative relationships and experimental evidence.
solution: Credit distinct supported points including: (1) Matter consists of particles whose arrangement, motion and attractions differ between solids, liquids and gases. (2) Heating raises average kinetic energy; a change of state occurs when energy changes intermolecular organization rather than chemical identity. (3) Gases are compressible because their particles occupy a small fraction of the container volume and are widely separated. (4) Diffusion becomes faster at higher temperature because particles move faster on average. (5) the calculation method illustrated by 1.00 mol.
questions.subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

questions.label: Hard
body: Evaluate the explanatory power and limitations of models used for introduction to the particulate nature of matter.
solution: Use particulate diagrams and energy ideas to distinguish physical changes, chemical changes and mixtures.
questions.subtopic: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of the nuclear atom.
solution: Atomic number equals proton number, while isotopes of an element have the same proton number but different neutron numbers.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in the nuclear atom.
solution: Mass spectra separate ions according to mass-to-charge ratio and isotope abundance can be used to calculate relative atomic mass.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to the nuclear atom.
solution: Nearly all atomic mass is concentrated in the tiny nucleus, while electrons occupy the surrounding volume.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of the nuclear atom to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Radioisotopes can trace chemical pathways because isotopes of one element have similar chemistry but distinguishable nuclei.

questions.label: Hard
body: Chlorine is 75.8% Cl-35 and 24.2% Cl-37. Calculate its relative atomic mass.
solution: Ar = (35 x 0.758) + (37 x 0.242) = 35.484, so 35.5 to three significant figures.

questions.label: Medium
body: Identify and correct one common misconception about the nuclear atom.
solution:
For example, reject: Isotopes of one element have different numbers of protons.
Correct account: Atomic number equals proton number, while isotopes of an element have the same proton number but different neutron numbers.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare count rate from a radioactive source at different distances. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable.
solution:
Independent: distance from the source.
Dependent: corrected count rate.
Controlled: counting time and source activity.

questions.label: Hard
body: Predict the trend expected in the investigation to compare count rate from a radioactive source at different distances and explain its chemical basis.
solution:
Expected trend: count rate should decrease as distance increases.
The explanation should use the model or relationship: Mass spectra separate ions according to mass-to-charge ratio and isotope abundance can be used to calculate relative atomic mass.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss the nuclear atom, integrating particulate or structural models, quantitative relationships and experimental evidence.
solution: Credit distinct supported points including: (1) Atomic number equals proton number, while isotopes of an element have the same proton number but different neutron numbers. (2) Mass spectra separate ions according to mass-to-charge ratio and isotope abundance can be used to calculate relative atomic mass. (3) Nearly all atomic mass is concentrated in the tiny nucleus, while electrons occupy the surrounding volume. (4) Radioisotopes can trace chemical pathways because isotopes of one element have similar chemistry but distinguishable nuclei. (5) the calculation method illustrated by 35.5.

questions.label: Hard
body: Evaluate the explanatory power and limitations of models used for the nuclear atom.
solution: Connect nuclear composition, isotopic abundance, mass spectra and the uses and risks of radioisotopes.

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of electron configurations.
solution: Electrons occupy quantized energy levels and orbitals, with lower-energy orbitals filled before higher-energy orbitals.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in electron configurations.
solution: An emission spectrum forms when excited electrons fall to lower levels and emit photons with energies equal to level differences.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to electron configurations.
solution: Valence-electron configuration helps explain periodic chemical behaviour and common ion charges.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of electron configurations to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Successive ionization requires energy, and a large jump indicates removal from a lower principal energy level.

questions.label: Hard
body: State the ground-state electron configuration of Na (Z = 11).
solution: Fill orbitals in increasing energy order: 1s2 2s2 2p6 accounts for 10 electrons; the eleventh enters 3s. Configuration: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1.

questions.label: Medium
body: Identify and correct one common misconception about electron configurations.
solution:
For example, reject: Electrons can possess any energy within an atom.
Correct account: Electrons occupy quantized energy levels and orbitals, with lower-energy orbitals filled before higher-energy orbitals.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will record emission wavelengths from excited gas samples. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable.
solution:
Independent: identity of the gas.
Dependent: set of emission wavelengths.
Controlled: discharge voltage and spectrometer calibration.

questions.label: Hard
body: Predict the trend expected in the investigation to record emission wavelengths from excited gas samples and explain its chemical basis.
solution:
Expected trend: each element should produce a characteristic line spectrum.
The explanation should use the model or relationship: An emission spectrum forms when excited electrons fall to lower levels and emit photons with energies equal to level differences.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss electron configurations, integrating particulate or structural models, quantitative relationships and experimental evidence.
solution: Credit distinct supported points including: (1) Electrons occupy quantized energy levels and orbitals, with lower-energy orbitals filled before higher-energy orbitals. (2) An emission spectrum forms when excited electrons fall to lower levels and emit photons with energies equal to level differences. (3) Valence-electron configuration helps explain periodic chemical behaviour and common ion charges. (4) Successive ionization requires energy, and a large jump indicates removal from a lower principal energy level. (5) the calculation method illustrated by 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1.

questions.label: Hard
body: Evaluate the explanatory power and limitations of models used for electron configurations.
solution: Relate electron arrangements and energy transitions to spectra, periodicity, ion formation and chemical identity.

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of counting particles by mass: the mole.
solution: One mole contains Avogadro's constant of specified entities and links particle number to measurable mass.
questions.subtopic: Counting particles by mass: the mole

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in counting particles by mass: the mole.
solution: Balanced equations give mole ratios; limiting reactant determines the maximum theoretical amount of product.
questions.subtopic: Counting particles by mass: the mole

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to counting particles by mass: the mole.
solution: Empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio, whereas molecular formula gives the actual number of each atom.
questions.subtopic: Counting particles by mass: the mole

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of counting particles by mass: the mole to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Percentage yield compares actual yield with theoretical yield and cannot diagnose the cause of product loss by itself.
questions.subtopic: Counting particles by mass: the mole

questions.label: Hard
body: Calculate the number of moles in 11.7 g NaCl using M = 58.5 g mol-1.
solution: n = m/M = 11.7 g / 58.5 g mol-1 = 0.200 mol.
questions.subtopic: Counting particles by mass: the mole

questions.label: Medium
body: Identify and correct one common misconception about counting particles by mass: the mole.
solution:
For example, reject: Molar mass is measured in moles per gram.
Correct account: One mole contains Avogadro's constant of specified entities and links particle number to measurable mass.
questions.subtopic: Counting particles by mass: the mole

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will determine the empirical formula of an oxide by heating a metal in air. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable.
solution:
Independent: initial amount of metal.
Dependent: mass increase due to oxygen.
Controlled: heating time after constant mass is reached.
questions.subtopic: Counting particles by mass: the mole

questions.label: Hard
body: Predict the trend expected in the investigation to determine the empirical formula of an oxide by heating a metal in air and explain its chemical basis.
solution:
Expected trend: oxygen gained should be proportional to the amount of metal that reacts completely.
The explanation should use the model or relationship: Balanced equations give mole ratios; limiting reactant determines the maximum theoretical amount of product.
questions.subtopic: Counting particles by mass: the mole

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss counting particles by mass: the mole, integrating particulate or structural models, quantitative relationships and experimental evidence.
solution: Credit distinct supported points including: (1) One mole contains Avogadro's constant of specified entities and links particle number to measurable mass. (2) Balanced equations give mole ratios; limiting reactant determines the maximum theoretical amount of product. (3) Empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio, whereas molecular formula gives the actual number of each atom. (4) Percentage yield compares actual yield with theoretical yield and cannot diagnose the cause of product loss by itself. (5) the calculation method illustrated by 0.200 mol.

questions.label: Hard
body: Evaluate the explanatory power and limitations of models used for counting particles by mass: the mole.
solution: Solve a multistep stoichiometric problem including limiting reactant, theoretical yield, excess and uncertainty.
questions.subtopic: Counting particles by mass: the mole

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of ideal gases.
solution: An ideal gas model assumes negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces and elastic collisions.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in ideal gases.
solution: Gas pressure results from particle collisions with container walls; temperature in kelvin tracks average translational kinetic energy.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to ideal gases.
solution: At constant temperature and amount, pressure is inversely proportional to volume.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of ideal gases to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Real gases deviate most at high pressure and low temperature because particle volume and attractions become significant.

questions.label: Hard
body: Calculate the pressure of 0.500 mol gas in 12.0 dm3 at 298 K using R = 8.31 kPa dm3 mol-1 K-1.
solution: P = nRT/V = (0.500 mol)(8.31 kPa dm3 mol-1 K-1)(298 K)/(12.0 dm3) = 103 kPa.

questions.label: Medium
body: Identify and correct one common misconception about ideal gases.
solution:
For example, reject: Gas particles have strong attractions in the ideal model.
Correct account: An ideal gas model assumes negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces and elastic collisions.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure gas volume at different temperatures at constant external pressure. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable.
solution:
Independent: temperature in kelvin.
Dependent: gas volume.
Controlled: amount of gas and external pressure.

questions.label: Hard
body: Predict the trend expected in the investigation to measure gas volume at different temperatures at constant external pressure and explain its chemical basis.
solution: Expected trend: volume should increase approximately linearly with kelvin temperature. The explanation should use the model or relationship: Gas pressure results from particle collisions with container walls; temperature in kelvin tracks average translational kinetic energy.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss ideal gases, integrating particulate or structural models, quantitative relationships and experimental evidence.
solution: Credit distinct supported points including: (1) An ideal gas model assumes negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces and elastic collisions. (2) Gas pressure results from particle collisions with container walls; temperature in kelvin tracks average translational kinetic energy. (3) At constant temperature and amount, pressure is inversely proportional to volume. (4) Real gases deviate most at high pressure and low temperature because particle volume and attractions become significant. (5) the calculation method illustrated by 103 kPa.

questions.label: Hard
body: Evaluate the explanatory power and limitations of models used for ideal gases.
solution: Evaluate when the ideal gas equation is useful and explain deviations using the particulate model.

questions.label: Hard
body: Explain why the molecular-ion region can contain several peaks.
solution: Different isotope combinations produce ions with different masses, and some molecules fragment before detection.

questions.label: Hard
body: Use mass spectra and nuclear stability to extend the core model and evaluate its explanatory value.
solution:
Core extension: Fragmentation patterns and exact isotope peaks provide structural and isotopic evidence.
Relevant explanation: Different isotope combinations produce ions with different masses, and some molecules fragment before detection.

questions.label: Hard
body: Explain a large jump between successive ionization energies.
solution: After the valence electrons are removed, the next electron is taken from a lower shell closer to the nucleus.

questions.label: Hard
body: Use successive ionization and orbitals to extend the core model and evaluate its explanatory value.
solution:
Core extension: Successive ionization data reveal shell structure and valence-electron number.
Relevant explanation: After the valence electrons are removed, the next electron is taken from a lower shell closer to the nucleus.

questions.label: Hard
body: Explain why measured pressure can be below ideal pressure at moderate compression.
solution: Attractions pull particles away from the wall and reduce collision force or frequency.

questions.label: Hard
body: Use non-ideal gases to extend the core model and evaluate its explanatory value.
solution:
Core extension: The van der Waals corrections account qualitatively for attractions and finite particle volume.
Relevant explanation: Attractions pull particles away from the wall and reduce collision force or frequency.

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of the ionic model.
solution: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in an extended lattice.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in the ionic model.
solution: Ions form by electron transfer, and lattice stability increases with larger charge product and shorter ion separation.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to the ionic model.
solution: Ionic solids are brittle because shifting layers can bring like charges together and cause repulsion.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of the ionic model to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Molten or aqueous ionic substances conduct because ions can move, whereas ions are fixed in a solid lattice.

questions.label: Hard
body: Determine the formula of the compound formed from Al3+ and O2-.
solution: The least common multiple of charges 3 and 2 is 6: two Al3+ ions balance three O2- ions. Formula: Al2O3.

questions.label: Medium
body: Identify and correct one common misconception about the ionic model.
solution:
For example, reject: Ionic compounds consist of separate neutral molecules.
Correct account: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in an extended lattice.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare electrical conductivity of an ionic solid, its melt and its aqueous solution. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable.
solution:
Independent: physical state.
Dependent: electrical conductivity.
Controlled: amount and purity of the compound.

questions.label: Hard
body: Predict the trend expected in the investigation to compare electrical conductivity of an ionic solid, its melt and its aqueous solution and explain its chemical basis.
solution: Expected trend: conductivity should be low in the solid and higher when ions are mobile. The explanation should use the model or relationship: Ions form by electron transfer, and lattice stability increases with larger charge product and shorter ion separation.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss the ionic model, integrating particulate or structural models, quantitative relationships and experimental evidence.
solution: Credit distinct supported points including: (1) Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in an extended lattice. (2) Ions form by electron transfer, and lattice stability increases with larger charge product and shorter ion separation. (3) Ionic solids are brittle because shifting layers can bring like charges together and cause repulsion. (4) Molten or aqueous ionic substances conduct because ions can move, whereas ions are fixed in a solid lattice. (5) the calculation method illustrated by Al2O3.

questions.label: Hard
body: Evaluate the explanatory power and limitations of models used for the ionic model.
solution: Use the ionic model to explain formulae, lattice structure, melting point, solubility, brittleness and conductivity.

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of the covalent model.
solution: A covalent bond is electrostatic attraction between a shared electron pair and two positive nuclei.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in the covalent model.
solution: Lewis structures, electron-domain repulsion and electronegativity help predict connectivity, shape and bond polarity.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to the covalent model.
solution: Molecular polarity depends on both bond dipoles and molecular geometry; polar bonds can cancel in a symmetric molecule.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of the covalent model to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Stronger intermolecular attractions generally increase boiling point when molecular size and shape are comparable.

questions.label: Hard
body: Predict the shape and approximate bond angle of CH4.
solution: CH4 has four bonding electron domains and no lone pairs around carbon. Electron-domain repulsion gives tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees.

questions.label: Medium
body: Identify and correct one common misconception about the covalent model.
solution:
For example, reject: A double bond contains fewer shared electrons than a single bond.
Correct account: A covalent bond is electrostatic attraction between a shared electron pair and two positive nuclei.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare boiling points across a homologous series. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable.
solution:
Independent: molar mass or chain length.
Dependent: boiling point.
Controlled: functional group and pressure.

questions.label: Hard
body: Predict the trend expected in the investigation to compare boiling points across a homologous series and explain its chemical basis.
solution: Expected trend: boiling point should generally rise as dispersion forces become stronger. The explanation should use the model or relationship: Lewis structures, electron-domain repulsion and electronegativity help predict connectivity, shape and bond polarity.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss the covalent model, integrating particulate or structural models, quantitative relationships and experimental evidence.
solution: Credit distinct supported points including: (1) A covalent bond is electrostatic attraction between a shared electron pair and two positive nuclei. (2) Lewis structures, electron-domain repulsion and electronegativity help predict connectivity, shape and bond polarity. (3) Molecular polarity depends on both bond dipoles and molecular geometry; polar bonds can cancel in a symmetric molecule. (4) Stronger intermolecular attractions generally increase boiling point when molecular size and shape are comparable. (5) the calculation method illustrated by tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees.

questions.label: Hard
body: Evaluate the explanatory power and limitations of models used for the covalent model.
solution: Relate Lewis structures, resonance, shape, polarity and intermolecular forces to physical properties and reactivity.

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of the metallic model.
solution: Metallic bonding is attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized valence electrons.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in the metallic model.
solution: Delocalized electrons carry charge and thermal energy through the lattice while non-directional bonding permits layers to slide.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to the metallic model.
solution: Metallic lattices are malleable because displacement does not necessarily place like localized charges directly beside one another.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of the metallic model to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Alloying can increase hardness by introducing atoms of different sizes that hinder layer movement.

questions.label: Hard
body: Which model best explains copper's electrical conductivity?
solution: Copper contains mobile delocalized electrons that drift through the metallic lattice when a potential difference is applied.

questions.label: Medium
body: Identify and correct one common misconception about the metallic model.
solution:
For example, reject: Metals contain freely moving positive ions.
Correct account: Metallic bonding is attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized valence electrons.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare electrical resistance of wires made from a pure metal and an alloy. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable.
solution:
Independent: material composition.
Dependent: electrical resistance.
Controlled: wire length, diameter and temperature.

questions.label: Hard
body: Predict the trend expected in the investigation to compare electrical resistance of wires made from a pure metal and an alloy and explain its chemical basis.
solution:
Expected trend: the alloy should usually have greater resistance because disorder scatters electrons.
The explanation should use the model or relationship: Delocalized electrons carry charge and thermal energy through the lattice while non-directional bonding permits layers to slide.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss the metallic model, integrating particulate or structural models, quantitative relationships and experimental evidence.
solution: Credit distinct supported points including: (1) Metallic bonding is attraction between positive metal ions and delocalized valence electrons. (2) Delocalized electrons carry charge and thermal energy through the lattice while non-directional bonding permits layers to slide. (3) Metallic lattices are malleable because displacement does not necessarily place like localized charges directly beside one another. (4) Alloying can increase hardness by introducing atoms of different sizes that hinder layer movement. (5) the calculation method illustrated by mobile delocalized electrons.

questions.label: Hard
body: Evaluate the explanatory power and limitations of models used for the metallic model.
solution: Use the metallic model to explain conductivity, malleability, melting behaviour and the properties of alloys.

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of from models to materials.
solution: Material properties emerge from bonding, structure and defects across microscopic and macroscopic scales.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in from models to materials.
solution: Network covalent solids have strong bonds throughout a lattice, while polymers contain long covalent chains with variable intermolecular attractions.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to from models to materials.
solution: Graphite conducts along layers because electrons are delocalized, whereas diamond lacks mobile charge carriers.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of from models to materials to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Changing polymer chain length, branching or cross-linking can alter strength, flexibility and softening behaviour.

questions.label: Hard
body: Which material is expected to have the highest melting point: CH4, NaCl, SiO2 or Ne?
solution: SiO2 is a network covalent solid; melting requires disruption of strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice.

questions.label: Medium
body: Identify and correct one common misconception about from models to materials.
solution:
For example, reject: All carbon allotropes have identical properties because they contain the same element.
Correct account: Material properties emerge from bonding, structure and defects across microscopic and macroscopic scales.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will measure tensile strength of polymer samples with different degrees of cross-linking. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable.
solution:
Independent: degree of cross-linking.
Dependent: maximum tensile stress.
Controlled: sample dimensions and strain rate.

questions.label: Hard
body: Predict the trend expected in the investigation to measure tensile strength of polymer samples with different degrees of cross-linking and explain its chemical basis.
solution:
Expected trend: moderate cross-linking should generally increase rigidity and tensile strength.
The explanation should use the model or relationship: Network covalent solids have strong bonds throughout a lattice, while polymers contain long covalent chains with variable intermolecular attractions.

questions.label: Hard
body: Discuss from models to materials, integrating particulate or structural models, quantitative relationships and experimental evidence.
solution: Credit distinct supported points including: (1) Material properties emerge from bonding, structure and defects across microscopic and macroscopic scales. (2) Network covalent solids have strong bonds throughout a lattice, while polymers contain long covalent chains with variable intermolecular attractions. (3) Graphite conducts along layers because electrons are delocalized, whereas diamond lacks mobile charge carriers. (4) Changing polymer chain length, branching or cross-linking can alter strength, flexibility and softening behaviour. (5) the calculation method illustrated by SiO2.

questions.label: Hard
body: Evaluate the explanatory power and limitations of models used for from models to materials.
solution: Compare ionic, metallic, molecular, network and polymeric materials using structure-property evidence and model limitations.

questions.label: Hard
body: Explain why carbonate has three equal C-O bond lengths.
solution: Pi electron density is delocalized over three C-O bonds, making the bonds equivalent.

questions.label: Hard
body: Use formal charge, resonance and hybridization to extend the core model and evaluate its explanatory value.
solution:
Core extension: Resonance structures are alternative electron-pair representations of one delocalized structure.
Relevant explanation: Pi electron density is delocalized over three C-O bonds, making the bonds equivalent.

questions.label: Hard
body: Explain how doping can increase semiconductor conductivity.
solution: Added atoms introduce charge carriers or accessible energy states, increasing mobile carrier concentration.

questions.label: Hard
body: Use advanced materials to extend the core model and evaluate its explanatory value.
solution: Core extension: Band structure, doping and nanoscale dimensions can tune material properties. Relevant explanation: Added atoms introduce charge carriers or accessible energy states, increasing mobile carrier concentration.

questions.label: Easy

solution: The periodic table arranges elements by proton number and reveals recurring valence-electron patterns.

questions.label: Medium

solution: Across a period, effective nuclear attraction generally increases while shielding changes little, causing atomic radius to decrease.

questions.label: Medium

solution: Elements in a group have related valence configurations and therefore show recurring chemical behaviour.

solution:
Independent: element or compound identity.
Dependent: pH or reaction rate.
Controlled: sample amount and water volume.

solution:
Expected trend: systematic changes should reflect changing metallic character and oxide acidity.

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of functional groups: classification of organic compounds.
solution: Organic compounds are classified by carbon skeleton and functional groups that influence naming, properties and reactions.
questions.subtopic: Functional groups: classification of organic compounds

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in functional groups: classification of organic compounds.
solution: Members of a homologous series share a functional group and general formula, with successive members differing by CH2.
questions.subtopic: Functional groups: classification of organic compounds

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to functional groups: classification of organic compounds.
solution: Hydrogen-bonding functional groups raise water solubility and boiling point relative to similar non-polar molecules.
questions.subtopic: Functional groups: classification of organic compounds

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of functional groups: classification of organic compounds to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity and may have different properties.
questions.subtopic: Functional groups: classification of organic compounds

questions.label: Hard

(4) Reaction conditions can favour different pathways, so identifying the functional group alone may not uniquely determine the product. (5) the calculation method illustrated by 1,2-dibromoethane.

solution: Classify organic transformations using structures, reagents, conditions, observations, atom economy and mechanism evidence.

questions.label: Easy
body: State a central principle of electron-pair sharing reactions.
solution: Lewis acids accept electron pairs and Lewis bases donate electron pairs to form coordinate covalent bonds.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain the model or mechanism used in electron-pair sharing reactions.
solution: Nucleophiles donate electron pairs to electron-deficient centres, while electrophiles accept electron pairs.

questions.label: Medium
body: Explain one structure-property relationship relevant to electron-pair sharing reactions.
solution: Curly arrows represent movement of electron pairs and must begin at an electron pair or bond.

questions.label: Medium
body: Apply knowledge of electron-pair sharing reactions to explain a chemical observation or prediction.
solution: Lone-pair availability and charge influence nucleophilicity and Lewis acid-base interactions.

questions.label: Hard
body: Which species acts as the Lewis base in BF3 + NH3 to form F3B-NH3?
solution: NH3 donates its nitrogen lone pair to electron-deficient BF3, so the Lewis base is NH3.

questions.label: Medium
body: Identify and correct one common misconception about electron-pair sharing reactions.
solution:
For example, reject: A nucleophile accepts an electron pair.
Correct account: Lewis acids accept electron pairs and Lewis bases donate electron pairs to form coordinate covalent bonds.

questions.label: Hard
body: A student will compare substitution rate with different nucleophile concentrations. Identify the independent, dependent and one controlled variable.
solution:
Independent: nucleophile concentration.
Dependent: initial substitution rate.
Controlled: substrate concentration and solvent.

questions.label: Hard

solution:
Expected trend: rate may rise with nucleophile concentration when the nucleophile participates in the rate-determining step.
The explanation should use the model or relationship: Nucleophiles donate electron pairs to electron-deficient centres, while electrophiles accept electron pairs.

solution: Ethanoate ions react with added H+ to form weakly ionized ethanoic acid.

solution:

body: Explain why overall yield falls across a multistep synthesis.
solution: Each step has a yield below 100%, so multiplying step yields gives a smaller overall fraction.
